subject: physiology
title: The Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation and Acid-Base Buffers

steps.tx: Physiological acid-base equilibrium in extracellular fluid is dictated mathematically by the fundamental **Henderson-Hasselbalch equation**. This logarithmic relationship links systemic arterial blood pH directly to the dissociation constant of carbonic acid and the ratio of serum bicarbonate concentration to dissolved arterial carbon dioxide tension.
steps.say: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation calculates blood pH from the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide.

left.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
points: pKa of carbonic acid buffer in human blood = 6.10
Solubility coefficient (α) of CO2 in plasma = 0.03 mmHg^-1

steps.tx: Maintaining systemic arterial pH within the narrow physiological range of seven point three five to seven point four five depends on the crucial **twenty-to-one bicarbonate ratio**. Even if absolute values deviate, systemic blood pH remains precisely seven point four zero as long as the ratio of metabolic bicarbonate to respiratory carbon dioxide is preserved.
steps.say: Blood pH stays normal as long as the ratio of bicarbonate to carbon dioxide is maintained at twenty to one.

nodes.label: Metabolic Component: Regulated by Kidneys via [HCO3-] Reclamation (~24 mEq/L)
Respiratory Component: Regulated by Lungs via Alveolar PaCO2 Ventilation (~40 mmHg)
Logarithmic Henderson-Hasselbalch Output: Arterial pH = 6.1 + log(20) = 7.40

steps.tx: The extracellular fluid is defended against acute pH shifts by three major chemical buffering systems. The primary open buffer is the **carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system**, possessing infinite buffering capacity because volatile carbon dioxide is continually exhaled by alveolar ventilation while non-volatile bicarbonate is regenerated by the kidneys.
steps.say: The bicarbonate buffer system is extraordinarily effective because the lungs can rapidly exhale excess volatile carbon dioxide.

rows: Primary open buffer; carbon dioxide volatile clearance via lungs
Ideal physiological pKa; major titratable acid buffer in urine
Histidine imidazole rings provide massive intracellular buffer reserve
Adaptive buffer that expands tenfold during chronic metabolic acidosis

steps.tx: While bicarbonate dominates plasma, urinary acidification relies heavily on the **phosphate buffer system**, comprising dibasic and monobasic inorganic phosphate. Possessing a pKa of six point eight, filtered phosphate serves as the primary titratable acid in tubular fluid, buffering secreted protons without lowering tubular pH below critical thresholds.
steps.say: Filtered inorganic phosphate serves as the main titratable acid buffer, buffering hydrogen ions in tubular urine.

nodes.label: Filtered Dibasic Phosphate (HPO4 2-) Enters Renal Tubular Lumen
Type A Intercalated Cell Pumps Secreted H+ into Lumen via H+-ATPase
Proton Binds Dibasic Phosphate -> Forms Monobasic Phosphate (H2PO4 -)
Titratable Acid Excreted in Urine; Generates New Bicarbonate for Blood

steps.tx: Under conditions of severe chronic metabolic acidosis, phosphate excretion reaches a fixed ceiling, shifting the burden of proton excretion to the **ammonia buffer system**. Synthesized from glutamine in proximal tubular cells, non-ionic ammonia diffuses into the tubular lumen, trapping protons as ammonium ions that cannot diffuse back.
steps.say: The ammonia buffer system expands dramatically in chronic acidosis, synthesizing ammonium from glutamine to excrete acid.

left.title: Titratable Acid Excretion
points: Measured by titrating urine back to pH 7.4 with strong base (NaOH)
Fixed capacity limited by daily dietary phosphate filtration (~20 to 30 mEq/day)
Cannot expand significantly during severe chronic acidosis

right.title: Ammonium Excretion (NH4+)
points: Synthesized from glutamine via proximal tubule glutaminase
Basal excretion ~30 to 50 mEq/day in healthy adults
Adaptively increases up to 300 to 500 mEq/day in severe acidosis
Serves as the primary variable renal defense against chronic acid loads

steps.tx: Total net renal acid excretion equals the sum of titratable acid and urinary ammonium excretion minus any excreted bicarbonate. Because each excreted proton corresponds to one new bicarbonate ion added to systemic circulation, **net acid excretion** precisely balances daily metabolic non-volatile acid production under steady-state conditions.
steps.say: Net acid excretion equals titratable acid plus ammonium minus filtered bicarbonate, generating new bicarbonate for the body.

rows: Adds new bicarbonate to blood plasma
Adds new bicarbonate to blood plasma
Precisely neutralizes daily non-volatile sulfuric and phosphoric acids

steps.tx: Accumulation of fixed non-volatile acids from diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure lowers plasma bicarbonate, precipitating **metabolic acidosis**. Central chemoreceptors detect secondary hypercapnic shifts, eliciting deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations that lower arterial carbon dioxide partial pressure in respiratory compensation.
steps.say: Metabolic acidosis lowers bicarbonate, triggering rapid Kussmaul breathing to exhale carbon dioxide in compensation.

steps.tx: Failure of proximal tubular bicarbonate reclamation or distal proton excretion causes renal tubular acidosis. In distal type 1 RTA, intercalated cells fail to acidify urine below pH five point five, leading to **hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis** with a normal serum anion gap and high nephrolithiasis risk.
steps.say: Distal renal tubular acidosis prevents intercalated cells from acidifying urine, causing normal anion gap acidosis and kidney stones.
